evidence.title: Effect of use of ambient listening technology on patient-reported communication and satisfaction ratings
evidence.venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
evidence.outcome: Patient experience and satisfaction with AI-enabled visits measured with patient surveys in a pilot evaluation
evidence.effect: Among 31,917 surveys (7,164 pilot; 24,753 control), no significant difference in pre-post change in patient ratings between pilot and control physicians.
evidence.quote: We did not find evidence of AI scribes worsening or enhancing patient experiences.

evidence.title: Development and pilot testing of AYA-RISE, a risk information and screening education intervention for adolescents and young adults with cancer risk syndromes
evidence.outcome: Acceptability (AIM score) and distress after using the AYA-RISE chatbot
evidence.effect: Acceptability threshold exceeded, with post-test AIM score >4 by 80% of AYAs; no significant change in distress thermometer scores (pre 3.4, post 3.6, p=.34).
evidence.quote: Our threshold for acceptability was exceeded, with a post-test Acceptability of Intervention Measure (AIM) score of > 4 by 80% of AYAs.

evidence.title: Comparing the Acceptability and Quality of Intervention Modalities for Suicidality in the Emergency Department: Randomized Feasibility Trial
evidence.outcome: Patient-reported acceptability and appropriateness of chatbot-guided safety planning
evidence.effect: Self-administered acceptability median 4.00 (3.81-4.56); appropriateness 4.25 (3.75-4.25). Across modalities, H=3.90, P=.14 and H=1.05, P=.59, respectively.
evidence.quote: Participants rated the acceptability and appropriateness of ReachCare in the ED highly, with no significant difference across the 3 delivery modalities.

evidence.title: An LLM chatbot to facilitate primary-to-specialist care transitions: a randomized controlled trial
evidence.effect: Patient satisfaction was 3.99 ± 0.69 versus 3.41 ± 0.98 with usual care; P < 0.001; relative increase 17.0%, 95% CI 14.3–19.6.
evidence.quote: Patients and care partners in the PreA-only group reported significantly improved consultation experiences compared to the No-PreA group across the primary outcome, ease of communication: 3.99 ± 0.62 versus 3.44 ± 0.97; P < 0.001; relative increase 16.0%, 95% CI 13.5–18.5) and the four secondary outcomes: perceived physician attentiveness: 3.87 ± 0.85 versus 3.36 ± 1.04; P < 0.001; relative increase 15.1%, 95% CI 12.1–18.1), interpersonal regard (4.02 ± 0.73 versus 3.43 ± 1.05; P < 0.001; relative increase 17.2%, 95% CI 14.4–20.0), patient satisfaction (3.99 ± 0.69 versus 3.41 ± 0.98; P < 0.001; relative increase 17.0%, 95% CI 14.3–19.6) and future acceptability (3.79 ± 1.06 versus 2.81 ± 1.26; P < 0.001; relative increase 34.7%, 95% CI 30.4–39.1; Fig. 3a ).

evidence.title: AI at the bedside: Randomised controlled trial of ChatGPT's impact on student performance in real-patient clinical exams
evidence.outcome: Patient acceptance and satisfaction with student ChatGPT use
evidence.effect: Patients expressed high acceptance and satisfaction; numerical results and between-group comparisons were not reported.
evidence.quote: Patients expressed high acceptance and satisfaction with student ChatGPT use.

evidence.title: Chatbot Use by Patients Seeking Urogynecologic Consultation: A Randomized Trial
evidence.outcome: Patient visit satisfaction following peri-visit chatbot use
evidence.effect: Visit satisfaction was similar between groups; numerical satisfaction results were not reported.
evidence.quote: Understanding of diagnosis, visit satisfaction, and chatbot satisfaction were similar between groups.

evidence.title: Patient and dermatologists' perspectives on augmented intelligence for melanoma screening: A prospective study
evidence.venue: Journal of the European Academy of Dermatology and Venereology : JEADV
evidence.outcome: Patient-reported feeling of safety following AI, dermatologist, and augmented-intelligence screening
evidence.effect: Mean subjective safety scores were 9.5 with augmented intelligence, 7.7 with AI alone, and 9.1 with dermatologist alone; augmented intelligence exceeded AI (p < 0.0001) and dermatologist screening (p = 0.001).
evidence.quote: Regarding SSS, AuI induced a significantly higher feeling of safety than AI (mean-SSS (mSSS): 9.5 vs. 7.7, p < 0.0001) or dermatologist screening alone (mSSS: 9.5 vs. 9.1, p = 0.001).

evidence.title: Evaluation of the Effectiveness, Safety, and Patient Satisfaction of Artificial Intelligence-Based Patient Education and Counseling for Both Recipients and Donors in the Preoperative and Postoperative Phases of Organ Transplantation
evidence.outcome: Patient satisfaction with AI-supported education system measured by validated SAPS form
evidence.effect: 99.5% of patients expressed satisfaction with the AI-supported education system.
evidence.quote: Patient satisfaction was overwhelmingly positive, with 99.5% expressing satisfaction.

evidence.title: Informed Consent for Ambient Documentation Using Generative AI in Ambulatory Care
evidence.outcome: Patient-reported anticipated self-censorship during sensitive discussions with ambient documentation
evidence.effect: Patients reported anticipated self-censorship when discussing mental health (36 [35.0%]), sexual health (42 [40.8%]), or illicit activity (53 [51.5%]).
evidence.quote: However, patients were more likely to censor what they said when discussing mental health (36 [35.0%]), sexual health (42 [40.8%]), or illicit activity (53 [51.5%]).

evidence.title: Ambient AI Documentation and Patient Satisfaction in Outpatient Care: Retrospective Pilot Study
evidence.outcome: Press Ganey patient experience scores before vs after provider DAX ambient scribe use
evidence.effect: Scores rose on all items: provider concern +1.9 (P=.01), overall experience +1.3 (P=.09), likelihood to recommend +0.9 (P=.33); no decline in patient experience observed.
evidence.quote: Care provider concern for a patient's questions or worries increased the most (1.9 points; P=.01), followed by overall assessment of the experience (1.3 points; P=.09) and likelihood of recommending the provider (0.9 points; P=.33).

evidence.title: Evaluating the usability and practicality of AI-enabled smartphone-based obstetric ultrasound in Sierra Leone: a mixed-methods study
evidence.outcome: Client experience of ultrasound-enabled antenatal care
evidence.effect: Clients trusted scan results but reported absent counselling and poor communication. Combined ANC assessments and scanning averaged 3–5 min versus the 30–40 min recommended standard.
evidence.quote: Clients expressed frustration with the lack of communication and support.

evidence.title: Enhancing Public Healthcare with IoT and AI: A Comprehensive Study on Improving Dry Eye Disease Diagnosis
evidence.effect: SE satisfaction decreased 95.5 to 84.7; MQ satisfaction increased 73.4 to 96.7.
evidence.quote: In-depth analysis shows a decrease in SE satisfaction (95.5 to 84.7) and a substantial increase in MQ satisfaction (73.4 to 96.7) with prompted queries.

commentary.bottom_line: One controlled deployment study measured patient experience across 31,917 surveys and found no difference attributable to AI, and one 10-person pilot met an acceptability threshold, but no study tests whether measuring experience detects or prevents harm. Hazard studies suggest that some problems, such as patients withholding sensitive information, may not appear in general satisfaction scores.

perspectives.view: Two deployment studies measured patient experience with AI services. A quasi-experimental comparison of 31,917 surveys found no significant difference in pre-post rating change between pilot and control physicians, and a 10-person pre-post pilot found 80% exceeded the acceptability threshold. Neither study tests whether measuring experience changes decisions or detects harm, so certainty is very low.

In a qualitative study, 35.0% to 51.5% of patients anticipated self-censoring about mental health, sexual health, or illicit activity with ambient documentation. Satisfaction in other studies was similar or higher with AI. This pattern suggests general satisfaction items may miss withheld information, a failure mode that tailored questions would need to target.

Press Ganey scores rose after ambient scribe use across 49 providers, with only provider concern reaching significance (+1.9, P=.01). Generic instruments are easy to reuse but were not built for AI-specific questions. In a Swiss screening study, feeling of safety scored 7.7 with AI alone versus 9.5 with augmented intelligence, which suggests tailored items can separate configurations.

Both studies that tested the practice were in the United States and reported no Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy subgroups. Hazard studies in China, Turkey, and Sierra Leone enrolled limited English proficiency, rural, or low-income patients. In Sierra Leone, clients trusted scan results but reported absent counselling. Survey validity across languages and literacy levels remains untested.

None of the five endorsing sources is a regulation or statute; three are commentaries and two are guidance or frameworks. One commentary calls for patient-reported outcome and experience measures developed with patient partners. The NIST profile excerpt addresses misuse testing rather than patient experience, so its support for this practice is indirect.

The largest test drew on 31,917 routine patient surveys, 7,164 from pilot physicians, which suggests existing survey programs can support comparisons against a control group with modest added effort. A pre-post design without controls, as in the 49-provider Press Ganey analysis, may attribute secular trends to the AI tool.

In Sierra Leone, combined antenatal assessments and scanning averaged 3 to 5 minutes against a 30 to 40 minute standard, and clients reported poor communication. Patients rated AI-alone skin screening lower on feeling of safety than dermatologist screening. Asking patients directly may be the main route by which such experiences reach decision makers.

commentary.research_gap: No study compares AI evaluations that include patient-experience measurement with evaluations that do not, and none tests whether standard satisfaction instruments detect specific harms such as self-censorship or lost counselling time. Controlled studies are needed that validate tailored survey items against observed outcomes and that report response rates and results by language, literacy, and insurance status.
commentary.underserved_note: Neither study that tested the practice reported including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Hazard studies with limited English proficiency, low-literacy, low-income, and rural patients came from outside the United States, so a health system cannot assume that validated English-language surveys capture experience in these groups or reach them at adequate rates.
